introduction-the-universal-debugging-map.core: The OSI model splits networking into seven layers, each with one job and a clean interface to the layers above and below. Real networks follow the simpler TCP/IP model, but OSI's value is as a debugging map. It lets you say "this is a layer 3 problem" and test layer by layer from the cable up, instead of guessing.

first_principles.problem: 'The website is down' could be a cable, a route, a firewall, TLS or the app, and the team checks randomly.
truths: Each layer depends on the one below.
Isolating the failing layer narrows the search.
derivation: Know each layer's **job and unit** (bit, frame, packet, segment).

analogy.title: A building's floors for troubleshooting
analogy.story: If the lift doesn't reach floor 7, check power in the basement before blaming the 7th-floor office.
analogy.breaks: Buildings have strict floors; real protocols blur layer boundaries.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Failure isolated to one layer in minutes.

check.q: Why is OSI still useful if real networks use TCP/IP?
check.a: It provides a precise mental map and vocabulary for isolating which part of the stack is failing.

the-7-layers-overview.core: Layer 1 (physical) moves bits over a medium. Layer 2 (data link) moves frames between neighbours using MAC addresses. Layer 3 (network) routes packets across networks using IP. Layer 4 (transport) delivers segments between processes using ports (TCP, UDP). Layers 5–6 handle sessions and data formats such as encryption, and layer 7 is the application protocol (HTTP, DNS).

first_principles.problem: An engineer confuses MAC and IP addresses and can't explain why a router changes one but not the other.
truths: Each layer has its own addressing.
Each layer has its own data unit.
Upper layers ride on lower ones.

analogy.title: Sending a parcel internationally
analogy.story: Road (L1), local van between depots (L2), international routing by country/city (L3), the specific recipient (L4), and the letter's language and content (L5–7).
analogy.breaks: Parcels keep one label; packets get new L2 headers at every hop.

example.title: Addresses per hop
flow: Laptop → router: src MAC laptop, dst MAC router, dst IP server
Router → ISP: new MACs, same IPs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: MACs change per hop; IPs stay end-to-end.

check.q: Which address changes at every router hop, MAC or IP?
check.a: The MAC (layer 2) address changes per hop; the IP (layer 3) stays the same end-to-end (absent NAT).

layer-1-2-the-hardware-layers.core: Layer 1 is signals: copper, fibre and radio, with speed, duplex and physical errors. Layer 2 frames those bits for a local segment. Ethernet frames carry source and destination MAC addresses; switches learn which MAC sits on which port and forward frames only there, while broadcasts flood the whole VLAN. Many 'network' problems are L1/L2: bad cables, duplex mismatches, VLAN misconfiguration and MAC flapping.

first_principles.problem: A server has intermittent packet loss traced to a duplex mismatch on the switch port.
truths: Physical faults show as errors and drops.
Broadcast domains are bounded by VLANs.

analogy.title: Roads and local postal sorting
analogy.story: The road surface (L1) must be sound; the local sorter (switch) learns which house is on which street.
analogy.breaks: Postmen don't flood every house with unknown mail; switches do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Physical issue identified before blaming the app.

code.text:
ethtool eth0 | grep -E 'Speed|Duplex|Link'
ip -s link show eth0     # RX errors, dropped, overrun
# rising CRC/RX errors → cable or duplex problem

check.q: What does a switch do with a frame for an unknown destination MAC?
check.a: It floods the frame out all ports in the VLAN except the one it arrived on.

layer-3-the-routing-layer.core: Layer 3 moves packets between networks. Each host has an IP address and subnet mask; destinations outside its subnet go to the default gateway. Routers forward each packet by longest-prefix match in their routing table, decrementing TTL to stop loops. ICMP reports problems. Typical L3 failures are missing routes, wrong masks, asymmetric routing and MTU or fragmentation issues.

first_principles.problem: A new subnet can reach the internet but not another VPC because a return route is missing.

analogy.title: Road signs at every junction
analogy.story: Each junction only knows which direction leads to a destination; the most specific sign wins.
analogy.breaks: Drivers can ask for directions; packets just follow tables.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See exact next hop and where packets die.

code.text:
ip route get 10.20.3.4
# 10.20.3.4 via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0 src 10.0.1.15
mtr -rwc 20 10.20.3.4    # where does it stop?

check.q: If routes 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.20.0.0/16 both match, which is used?
check.a: 10.20.0.0/16, because it is the longer, more specific prefix.

layer-4-the-transport-layer.core: Layer 4 delivers data between processes using ports. TCP provides reliable, ordered byte streams with handshakes, acknowledgements, retransmission, flow control and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and minimal overhead. Firewalls, load balancers and NAT mostly operate on the L4 5-tuple (protocol, source/destination IP and port).

first_principles.problem: A firewall rule allows TCP 53 but DNS still times out because most queries use UDP 53.

analogy.title: Apartment numbers and delivery types
analogy.story: The building (IP) is right, but you need the apartment (port) and whether you want signed-for (TCP) or drop-off (UDP).
analogy.breaks: Drop-offs are rarely lost; UDP packets often are.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows whether the port is listening and reachable per protocol.

code.text:
ss -ltnup | grep ':53'        # TCP and UDP listeners
nc -vz db.internal 5432       # TCP reachability
dig @10.0.0.2 example.com     # UDP DNS test

check.a: Protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port.

layers-5-6-session-and-presentation.core: In practice, layers 5 and 6 are folded into applications and libraries. Session concerns (establishing, maintaining and resuming conversations) show up as TLS sessions, RPC streams and authentication tokens. Presentation concerns (encoding, compression and encryption) show up as TLS, character sets, JSON and Protobuf serialisation. Bugs here look like 'connected but garbled' or 'handshake failed'.

first_principles.problem: A client connects to port 443 but fails with 'wrong version number' because it's speaking TLS to a plaintext port.
truths: Encryption and encoding sit between transport and app.

analogy.title: Language and envelope sealing
analogy.story: The letter arrives, but if it's sealed with a lock you can't open or written in a language you don't read, it's useless.
analogy.breaks: Letters don't renegotiate languages; TLS negotiates versions and ciphers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reveals handshake, cert and version issues.

code.text:
openssl s_client -connect api.acme.com:443 -servername api.acme.com </dev/null | head -20
# shows cert chain, protocol (TLSv1.3), cipher

check.q: Where does TLS fit in the OSI model?
check.a: Roughly layers 5–6: it manages secure sessions and encrypts/presents data between transport and application.

layer-7-the-application-layer.core: Layer 7 is the protocol the application speaks: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, gRPC. Problems here show up as status codes (404, 502, 503), protocol errors, wrong Host headers, auth failures or slow backends, even though every lower layer is fine. L7 proxies and load balancers can route by path, header or cookie, which makes them powerful and also a frequent source of misconfiguration.

first_principles.problem: curl to the server IP works but the site returns 404 because the request lacks the right Host header.
truths: Lower layers can be fine while L7 fails.
App protocols carry routing info (Host, path).

analogy.title: A correctly delivered letter addressed to the wrong person
analogy.story: It reached the building and the right flat, but the person named isn't there.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists ask; proxies follow rules exactly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proves the issue is virtual-host routing.

check.q: What does a 502 from a load balancer usually indicate?
check.a: The LB reached but got an invalid/no response from the upstream backend, an application or backend connectivity problem.

encapsulation-the-russian-dolls.core: Sending data wraps it layer by layer: application data gets a TCP header (segment), then an IP header (packet), then an Ethernet header and trailer (frame), then becomes bits. Each hop unwraps and rewraps only what it needs: switches look at L2, routers at L3. Every header costs bytes, which is why tunnels and overlays reduce the effective MTU.

first_principles.problem: Adding a VPN tunnel causes large transfers to hang because the encapsulation overhead pushes packets over the MTU.
truths: Devices read only their layer's header.

analogy.title: Russian dolls
analogy.story: Each layer is a doll around the previous one; each handler only opens the doll meant for them.
analogy.breaks: Dolls don't have size limits; frames do (MTU).

check.q: Why do tunnels reduce the maximum payload size?
check.a: They add extra headers inside the same physical MTU, leaving fewer bytes for the inner packet.

mapping-tools-to-layers.core: Each layer has go-to tools. L1/L2: ethtool, ip link, switch port counters, arp/ip neigh. L3: ping, traceroute/mtr, ip route. L4: ss, nc, telnet, nmap. L5/6: openssl s_client. L7: curl -v, dig, browser devtools. tcpdump and Wireshark span all layers. Knowing what each tool proves, and what it doesn't, avoids false conclusions such as 'ping works, so the port must be open'.

first_principles.problem: An engineer concludes the database is reachable because ping succeeds, but port 5432 is blocked.
truths: Success at one layer doesn't prove the next.

analogy.title: A doctor's diagnostic kit
analogy.story: A stethoscope says nothing about bones; you pick the instrument for the system you're examining.
analogy.breaks: Doctors combine results intuitively; be explicit about what each tool proves.

example.title: Ping isn't enough

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proves an L4 block, not an L3 outage.

code.text:
ping -c2 db.internal          # L3 OK
nc -vz db.internal 5432       # L4: Connection timed out → firewall
tcpdump -ni eth0 host db.internal and port 5432   # SYNs out, nothing back

example.outcome: the right tool for each layer.

check.q: What does a successful ping prove?
check.a: Only that ICMP echo works at layer 3 between the hosts; not that any specific TCP/UDP port is open.
